The finding admits this needs publish rights on the maintainer's release repo, through a stolen account or token. That repo is the product's trust root, not a surface an outside attacker can reach. The transport is locked down: HTTPS, a host allow-list for the DMG and checksum URLs (isAllowedDownloadURL, :182, :226), and a pinned HTTPClient (:239-241). So no network attacker or third party can inject a release. The DMG is only moved at :265 and revealed at :275, and the user still has to mount it, drag the app and launch it. Whoever can publish a release can also change the README and the release page, so the same attacker already reaches every new install. Missing quarantine and team-ID pinning would be defence in depth against a compromised trust root, not a reachable bypass in the default deployment. Quarantine alone would not stop a release signed with some other Developer ID anyway. The claimed attack path starts from a privileged-compromise premise, so the source is not attacker-controlled under the reachability lens.
